newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: EU calls for BSE beef aid worth one bln Ecus.
newsitem.headline: EU calls for BSE beef aid worth one bln Ecus.

text.p: European Union farm ministers called for a package of urgent measures worth one billion Ecus to aid farmers hit by the mad cow crisis and to help restore consumer confidence.

The package includes increasing and extending the scope of beef intervention purchases, calf slaughter and other production-reducing schemes, advancing aid payments and meat labelling, identification and promotion schemes.
"We are trying to come forward with the best possible solution," Irish Farm Minister Ivan Yates told a news conference after a three-day informal meeting.

EU Farm Commissioner Franz Fischler warned that the funding of the new aid plans, which supplement an earlier 850 million Ecus package of emergency measures finalised at an EU summit in Florence in June, still had to be sorted out.
"We are going to have to talk an awful lot yet about how to fund the package," Fischler said.

Yates, whose country holds the rotating EU presidency, said that member states were against the cost being financed by cuts in other sectors. He was referring to a Commission proposal for a seven percent cut in aid payments to cereals farmers.
Yates said a political agreement had been reached to ensure enough surplus beef would be taken into EU intervention stores in October and at the first tender in November.
Commission officials estimated around 100,000 tonnes of beef would be sold into storage during this period.

An extension of intervention buying was needed because a 400,000 tonne limit for 1996 was expected to be breached in early October and ministers were not due to meet again until the end of next month.
Beef stocks were virtually non-existent before the mad cow crisis erupted in March.

"If intervention hadn't been extended prices would have collapsed," said a Commission official, noting that October was a critical month as farmers tried to sell their herds after summer outdoor fattening.

The Commission had proposed raising the intervention ceiling to 720,000 tonnes in 1996 but this was opposed by some member states, notably Germany, which argued that this was an expensive and inefficient way of reducing production.
Intervention buying is also being extended to include young cattle of between seven and nine months.
These two new intervention measures are due to be formally adopted in October.

Ministers are due to decide at the end of October whether further measures to cut beef output, such as an EU-wide calf slaughtering scheme and reduction of carcass weights eligible for public storage, are cost-effective and controllable.
At present only Britain and Portugal operate calf culling schemes.

Ministers also backed bringing forward up to 500 million Ecus of 1997 beef and suckler cow aid payments into the current financial year ending on October 15, so easing farmers' severe cash flow problems.

To help revive beef demand, which has plunged by up to 40 percent in some countries, Fischler is due to propose an Wednesday an EU meat labelling and identification scheme that will show consumers where beef came from and how it was produced.
A 10-million-Ecus a year beef promotion scheme is also due to be expanded in a bid to restore sales in the EU single market and non-EU countries.
